evidence_quotes.quote: For this analysis, I focus on the patterns that emerge around household domestic water access, preferred sources for drinking, the subjective lived experiences of water insecurity including risk perceptions, and the daily work and social relationships involved in accessing water and hygiene practices.

Although not explored in depth in this article, such dynamics would include the local arrangements of social power involved in water access, as well as the larger political economic processes determining infrastructure funding and subjectivities involved in treated water access
I analyzed qualitative data with MAXQDA coding software using both grounded theory and in vivo coding

rationale: This ethnographic study examines cultural dimensions, interpersonal kin-based sharing networks, risk perceptions, and water-hauling practices shaping household water insecurity in Newtok, Alaska, an unpiped Yupik village. While institutional background factors (e.g., stalled village relocation, unused storage tanks, and a 10-gallon/day school water ration during plant shutdowns) are noted contextually, the author explicitly notes that political-economic and institutional infrastructure processes are not explored in depth, and no legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism is empirically analyzed (`NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM`). The primary empirical outcome is `effective_access`, focusing on domestic water quantity (1.91 gal/capita/day of treated water), seasonal supply intermittency when the storage tank runs dry, physical hauling/fetching burdens across treated and natural sources, and perceived water potability/quality. The design is `qualitative`, relying on 6 days of participant observation and semi-structured interviews (n=23) coded in MAXQDA, supplemented only by a descriptive community-wide per-capita consumption figure from monthly water plant logs.
